title: New York Ban AI Toys for 5 Years
content:
S.9408A/A.11144B Prohibits Manufacturing, Distribution and Sale of Internet-Connected AI Toys in New York
Governor Urges Families to Keep Safety and Privacy in Mind When Choosing Holiday Gifts
Governor Kathy Hochul today signed a bill establishing a five-year pause on AI chatbot toys. Building on the Governor’s first in the nation AI Companion safeguards, S.9408A/A.11144B will place a five-year moratorium on the manufacturing, distribution and sale of toys in New York with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, such as talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with kids. Since the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, Governor Hochul also urged parents and caregivers to consider the potential risks of AI chatbot toys before purchasing gifts for young children this holiday season.
“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Governor Hochul said. “As New York’s first mom governor, protecting our kids is deeply personal to me, and when unregulated artificial intelligence poses a threat, it’s my job to put New York families first.”
New York Attorney General Letitia James said, “AI chatbots in children’s toys are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk. As New York continues to lead the way in protecting kids from dangerous new technologies, my office will not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”
According to a national consumer watchdog that tested a sample of chatbot toys marketed to children ages 3-12, some talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave. These toys had few or no parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer the conversation continued. Additionally, some toys could record a child’s voice or scan their face.
Violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation that will be enforced by the Attorney General.
State Senator Andrew Gounardes said, “The rush to sell AI-powered toys to young children is just the latest chapter in what has become a repetitive story: Big Tech puts profits before kids’ safety, and families pay the price. But we don’t have to live in a Twilight Zone episode turned real. By pressing pause on the sale of AI chatbot toys for small children, we can take the time to study their impact on kids and create smart protections before more damage is done. It’s logical, it’s fair, and most importantly, it makes clear that our children’s safety is nothing for Big Tech to play around with.”
Assemblymember Rebecca Kassay said, “Consumer protections, especially those that protect our youth, must keep up with rapidly evolving technologies. I am proud to have worked with Senator Gounardes to champion this moratorium on the manufacture, exchange, distribution, and sale of AI-powered chatbot companion toys for children in New York, and grateful to Governor Hochul for signing this legislation. These toys, including dolls, robots, and stuffed animals, can mimic human characteristics and relationships while potentially collecting sensitive data, posing risks to children’s health and development without strong guardrails in place. This moratorium gives our state time to assess these emerging technologies and develop meaningful regulations on artificial intelligence in children’s toys. I applaud Governor Hochul and the nearly unanimous support of the Senate and Assembly in taking swift action to protect New York’s children.”
Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk."
Mothers Against Media Addiction (MAMA) Policy Director LaVita Tuff said, “Parents should be able to feel confident that the toys their children play with are safe, which means that toys containing AI should only be sold if they are safe by design. This holiday season, we at MAMA are grateful to Governor Hochul for signing this law and ensuring that toys sold in New York meet a high standard of safety. With this measure, New York continues leading the way to protect our kids in the age of AI.”
Common Sense Media Founder and CEO James P. Steyer said,“This moratorium on AI toys in New York could not come soon enough. Our research shows they aren’t safe for kids. We applaud Senator Gounardes, Governor Hochul, and Assemblymember Kassay, for passing this bill and signing it into law. And, parents should not wait for the moratorium to kick in - if you are getting toys for kids this holiday season, stick to traditional toys and toys that encourage social-emotional development and human engagement, not AI toys that undermine children’s development and risk their safety.”
With families preparing their holiday gift lists, Governor Hochul encouraged parents and caregivers to look beyond a toy’s packaging and consider whether it includes an AI companion, what information it collects, and whether it allows open ended conversation with a child. Although the moratorium will not be in effect this holiday season, the signing of this legislation highlights these concerns now, before families make purchasing decisions.
The signing of this bill builds upon Governor Hochul’s efforts to protect children from emerging technology risks. In October the Governor signed legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit conversations. This announcement also builds on Governor Hochul’s ongoing efforts to address the youth mental health crisis statewide and help keep kids safe online. This work has established New York as a global leader in securing a safer online world for children, and as of this year New York is ranked number one in the U.S. for laws that keep kids safe online.
Governor Hochul’s Record on Responsible AI
This announcement builds on Governor Hochul’s ongoing efforts to address the youth mental health crisis statewide and help keep kids safe online. This work has established New York as a global leader in securing a safer online world for children, and as of this year New York is ranked number one in the U.S. for laws that keep kids safe online. Initiatives include:
- The SAFE for Kids Act, which restricts addictive features of social media for kids, and established an important national precedent about age verification.
- The Child Data Protection Act that prevents online operators from collecting and monetizing children’s data without informed consent.
- The Governor also outlawed AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
- The Unplug and Play Agenda which helps encourage healthy socialization and child development by funding social infrastructure, physical sites like playgrounds, community centers, and pools, and expanded youth programming.
- New York’s Distraction Free Learning Policy, requiring statewide, bell-to-bell restrictions on smartphones in K-12 schools, which is already resulting in greater academic achievement, improved student wellbeing, and safer school environments for students.
- The Social Media Warning Labels bill that will require social media companies to post warnings about the platform's potential impact on mental health.
- The Safe by Design Act, which will protect kids from predatory behavior online and defaults them to the highest privacy settings.

report.summary: New York signed a five-year ban on selling internet-connected AI chatbot toys, citing child safety and privacy risks, with penalties up to $15,000 per day.
report.background: AI chatbot toys—talking dolls, robots, and stuffed animals—connect to the internet and large language models to hold open-ended conversations. They promise companionship and education but often lack strong parental controls, data safeguards, or age-appropriate guardrails. New York has moved aggressively on child online safety, including the SAFE for Kids Act, the Child Data Protection Act, and restrictions on unsafe chatbot features for minors. The bill reflects growing concern that consumer AI is outpacing toy-safety rules and federal privacy enforcement. It also follows consumer-watchdog testing that found inappropriate content and weak safeguards in some toys marketed to young children. The five-year pause is meant to give regulators time to study developmental and privacy impacts and craft standards; it takes effect 90 days after signing, so it does not cover this holiday season.
key_points: The law imposes a five-year moratorium on manufacturing, distributing, or selling toys in New York that have embedded or integrated AI chatbots and use the internet to converse with children. It takes effect 90 days after signing, so this holiday season is not covered. Violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day per violation, enforced by the Attorney General.

The bill cites watchdog testing of chatbot toys marketed to children ages 3–12. Some discussed sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches, and acted upset when a child left. Toys had few or no parental controls, safety limits weakened over longer conversations, and some could record voices or scan faces. These findings drove the moratorium.

New York frames the ban as a pause, not a permanent prohibition. The goal is to study AI toys’ effects on child development and privacy and develop meaningful safety rules. Officials say the state can then allow compliant products with strong guardrails rather than unregulated open-ended chatbots.

The signing builds on Governor Hochul’s broader child-safety agenda: the SAFE for Kids Act, Child Data Protection Act, restrictions on addictive or sexually explicit chatbot features for minors, school phone limits, and social media warning labels. New York says it ranks first in the U.S. for laws protecting kids online.

The law does not block this season’s sales, so officials are urging parents to examine whether a toy includes an AI companion, what data it collects, and whether it allows open-ended conversation. Consumer groups recommend traditional toys that encourage human engagement rather than AI toys with weak safeguards.
report.impact: For the AI toy industry, New York’s ban creates a major compliance and market-access problem: manufacturers may withdraw products, restrict open-ended chat, or wait for standards. It also signals a state-by-state patchwork that could raise costs and encourage privacy-by-design. Developers should treat child-facing chatbots as high-risk, with strong moderation, data minimization, parental controls, and age-appropriate design. For regular users, New York families will see fewer such toys after the law takes effect, but this holiday season parents still need to check whether a toy records voice or faces, allows open-ended conversation, and has real controls. The law may push the market toward offline or narrowly scripted toys.
report.tools: Parents can check Common Sense Media reviews and Mozilla’s Privacy Not Included before buying connected toys. Developers can use open-source safety and moderation tools such as OpenAI Evals, Llama Guard/Purple Llama, and LangKit to test chatbot behavior; UNICEF’s AI for Children guidance and FTC COPPA resources help with child-privacy design. Watch for New York Attorney General enforcement guidance and any state-led standards for AI toys.
